metadata.title: Predicting the Mathematics Literacy of Resilient Students from High‐performing Economies: A Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata and restricts the analytic sample to resilient students defined within each economy using ESCS and mathematics literacy PVs. The authors incorporate final student weights (W_FSTUWT) during ML model development and nested cross-validation to adjust for PISA’s complex survey design features (stratification, clustering, and unequal selection probabilities), aiming for representativeness of the target student population within each culture group. Because the ML models are trained in R (caret) with weights included in the training/validation process, the reported predictive performance is intended to reflect population-level patterns rather than only the raw selected sample. No replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) is reported, so uncertainty quantification is not described via replicate designs.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is restricted to PISA 2022 15-year-old students from high-performing mathematics economies (economies with average mathematics literacy score > 472). Within each economy, students are first screened to the bottom quarter of ESCS (economic, social and cultural status) and then further selected to the top quarter of mathematics literacy within that economy. To define the top quarter of mathematics literacy, the authors compute an average of 10 plausible values (PV1–PV10) for mathematics literacy, rank students by this PV average, and select students in the top 25% of mathematics literacy while also meeting the bottom-25% ESCS criterion. Finally, the selected resilient students are grouped into two culture datasets (Eastern vs Western) based on Triandis’ (1995) cultural orientation, and ML models are trained separately within each culture group.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Eastern cultures)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics literacy (PV1–PV10 averaged; Random Forest prediction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (Eastern): RMSE (Average across PVs): 44.47 (Validation/Test averages reported per PV; e.g., PV1 average RMSE=44.47, R2=0.01, MAE=35.40). R2 values are low (e.g., PV1 average R2=0.01; PV7 average R2=0.02).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Eastern cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century and formal/applied), mathematics anxiety, effort/persistence, and working in the household to predict mathematics literacy, finding that Random Forest achieved lower error than Lasso in Eastern cultures (e.g., RMSE rank comparisons favored RF over LR). This indicates that strengthening self-efficacy and addressing mathematics anxiety alongside effort-supporting practices may be particularly important for improving mathematics literacy among socioeconomically disadvantaged resilient students in Eastern contexts, though the study is predictive and not causal.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Eastern cultures)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Lasso (Eastern): RMSE (Average across PVs): 45.96 (e.g., PV1 average RMSE=45.96, R2=0.00, MAE=36.44).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Eastern cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century and formal/applied), mathematics anxiety, effort/persistence, and working in the household to predict mathematics literacy, finding that Lasso regression underperformed Random Forest in Eastern cultures on RMSE/R2/MAE comparisons. This indicates that non-linear interactions among resilience-related psychosocial and contextual factors may be important in Eastern settings, suggesting that policy and practice should consider multi-factor support rather than relying on single linear predictors.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Western cultures)
main_findings.target_variable: Mathematics literacy (PV1–PV10 averaged; Random Forest prediction)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random Forest (Western): RMSE (Average across PVs): 42.27 (e.g., PV1 average RMSE=42.27, R2=0.06, MAE=32.65). R2 values remain modest (e.g., PV1 average R2=0.06; PV6 average R2=0.07).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Western cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (formal/applied), family support, home possessions, cognitive activation encouraging mathematical thinking, and mathematics anxiety to predict mathematics literacy, finding that Random Forest produced better predictive performance in Western cultures than in Eastern cultures (lower RMSE and higher R2 in Western vs Eastern). This indicates that interventions that boost mathematics self-efficacy and leverage supportive home and classroom environments may be effective for sustaining high mathematics literacy among disadvantaged resilient students in Western contexts, while causality cannot be inferred from the predictive ML design.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Western cultures)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Lasso (Western): RMSE (Average across PVs): 40.25 (e.g., PV1 average RMSE=40.25, R2=0.11, MAE=31.76).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Western cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (formal/applied), family support, home possessions, cognitive activation encouraging mathematical thinking, and mathematics anxiety to predict mathematics literacy, finding that Lasso regression achieved strong predictive fit in Western cultures (higher R2 and lower RMSE than in Eastern cultures). This indicates that linear, self-efficacy-centered and support-environment-focused strategies may align well with the dominant predictors of resilient mathematics literacy in Western contexts, though the results remain correlational/predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 mathematics literacy PVs to predict mathematics literacy among resilient students—defined within each economy as bottom-quarter ESCS and top-quarter mathematics literacy—then splits the sample into Eastern vs Western cultures. The analytic sample includes 4,654 students across 22 high-performing economies, with culture-group sample sizes of 3,591 (Western) and 1,063 (Eastern). Two supervised ML models are trained with nested cross-validation: Random Forest and Lasso regression, using final student weights (W_FSTUWT) during training/validation. Missing questionnaire data (0–26%) are imputed using missForest. Performance is evaluated with RMSE, R², and MAE across PV1–PV10; both models perform better in Western cultures than Eastern cultures (lower RMSE and higher R² in Western). Key predictors differ by culture: Eastern models emphasize mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century) and mathematics anxiety, while Western models emphasize mathematics self-efficacy (formal/applied) and supportive home/classroom factors. Limitations include predictive (not causal) inference and modest R² values, even when errors are reduced.
